hero.text: This app maps the global evidence base on health financing functions — studies that analyse how health systems raise, pool, allocate and spend money.
studies from the HSF extraction 29 Sept v5 are classified by the LLM extraction pipeline;
crosses any variables in the corpus, the
explains how the map is built.

No MeSH theme (no DOI or no match)

gallery.title: Size & growth
gallery.blurb: See how the health financing evidence base has grown since 2010 and how quickly new research is being published.

figs.title: Cumulative growth
figs.caption: Cumulative records analysed by publication year. Volume grew 28.8× since 2010 — half of all 34,258 records were published 2019 or later.

gallery.title: Financing functions & outcomes
gallery.blurb: Explore which parts of health financing are studied most, which outcomes they are linked to, and where important evidence gaps remain.

figs.title: Financing function
figs.caption: Studies by financing function — a study can carry more than one. Benefits decisions leads at 11,451 studies, 1.1× Public financial management's 10,044; capital-investment financing trails furthest behind.

figs.title: Financing-function mix over time
figs.caption: Share of tagged studies by year, top 5 functions, shown as separate lines; a study can carry more than one, so totals can exceed 100%. Benefits decisions's share moved only from 35% to 32% across the whole period — the alternative view tells the same story as the stacked bars.

figs.title: Financing-function output over time
figs.caption: Annual count of financing-function tags, by function (a study can carry more than one, so totals exceed the study count). Total tags grew 2.3× from 2010 to 2025; Benefits decisions's share moved from 25% to 22% of that total.

figs.title: Outcome domain
figs.caption: Alternative view: lollipop chart of studies by outcome domain — a study can carry more than one. Other is tagged 4.0× as often as Efficiency in the use of resources (20,735 vs 5,181), the next largest domain.

figs.title: Function vs. outcome
figs.caption: Outcome-domain mix of each financing function's tagged studies (row shares; a study can carry more than one tag of either kind, so rows needn't sum to 100%). 81% of Recurrent financing (supply chain) studies report Other, its most common outcome.

gallery.title: Topics & themes
gallery.blurb: Discover the health issues, disease areas and wider research themes covered by the evidence, including which topics receive the most or least attention.

figs.title: Topic landscape
figs.caption: OpenAlex-style topic taxonomy - each radial bar is a subfield (length = studies), coloured by domain. 'Economics and Econometrics' leads at 8,174 studies, 2.2× the next-largest ('Finance', 3,710); Social Sciences accounts for 15,266 of 29,697 studies with a topic label.

figs.title: Topic landscape (treemap)
figs.caption: Same OpenAlex-style topic taxonomy as the ranked chart, laid out as a treemap — each rectangle is a subfield (area = studies), grouped and coloured by field/domain. 'Economics and Econometrics' is 28% of 29,697 tagged studies on its own, 2.2× the next-largest subfield ('Finance', 3,710) — proportional area makes that concentration immediately visible.

figs.title: The opportunity matrix
figs.caption: For each MeSH-derived disease category, its share of tags for a given financing function, divided by that function's overall share across all disease-tagged studies. Blue = disproportionately more attention; red = disproportionately less. Injuries studies are tagged Purchasing 2.1× as often as the disease-tagged average, while Neurological & mental studies are tagged Recurrent financing (supply chain) only 0.32× as often — the widest gaps in either direction.

figs.title: How each disease area is evaluated
figs.caption: Mix of financing-function tags within each MeSH-derived disease category (row shares; a study can carry more than one tag, so rows needn't sum to 100%). Skin leans hardest on Benefits decisions (65% of its tagged studies).

figs.title: The disease focus of HFF research
figs.caption: Each bar is a MeSH-derived disease category; length is its share of the disease-coded literature, colour is whether that research skews toward richer or poorer countries. Maternal & neonatal research skews most toward L&MICs (68% L&MICs); Neurological & mental skews most toward high-income settings (92% high-income).

figs.title: L&MICs research: communicable to NCD shift
figs.caption: Disease mix of MeSH-classified HFF research about low- and middle-income countries, across three epidemiological-transition classes. Communicable/maternal/nutritional fell 80%→50%; non-communicable rose 20%→47%, 2010–2025.

figs.title: Evidence flow: design to function to outcome
figs.caption: Each ribbon is a group of studies flowing from study design, through primary financing function, to primary outcome domain (first-listed tag of each). Ribbon width is the study count. Benefits decisions is the largest single financing-function node (9,902 studies), feeding most often into Other (15,985 studies primarily reporting it).

figs.title: The disease atlas
figs.caption: HFF studies naming each country, split by MeSH-derived disease area (busiest first). Log scale. 'Infectious' research reaches the widest set of countries (111 named); several disease areas stay concentrated in a handful of systems.

figs.title: L&MICs research share, era 1 to era 2
figs.caption: Share of research about L&MICs within each MeSH-derived disease category, 2010–2017 (dot) to 2018–2026 (arrowhead). Chronic respiratory's L&MICs share rose +25pp; Infectious's fell -9pp — the widest swings either way.

figs.title: Thematic landscape
figs.caption: Abstract embeddings, UMAP + HDBSCAN - each point is one study, positioned by similarity. 'insurance / medicaid / medicare' is the largest emergent theme at 9,317 studies; the top 12 themes shown here cover about 64% of all topic-embedded studies.

figs.title: Top 20 research themes
figs.caption: Top 20 research themes, ranked by cluster size (keyword labels, not hand-assigned categories). 'insurance / medicaid / medicare' leads at 9,317 studies, 1.5× the next-largest ('patients / drug / drugs', 6,030).

figs.title: Themes by income skew
figs.caption: The emergent theme map, each theme coloured by the share of its single-country studies about L&MICs (overall 39%). 'insurance / vietnam / coverage' skews most L&MICs (100%); 'sud / treatment / substance' skews most high-income (100% high-income).

gallery.title: Methods & data
gallery.blurb: See how studies were designed, whether they used quantitative, qualitative or mixed methods, and what kinds of data they analysed.

figs.title: Methodological characteristics of included studies
figs.caption: Distribution of 36,495 studies by study design, data type and data source. Each study was assigned one category per dimension. Cross-sectional & correlational is the most common design (25%); cross-sectional data and administrative sources lead their dimensions (35% and 37%).

gallery.title: Geographic coverage
gallery.blurb: Where health financing research is concentrated: which countries, income groups and settings it covers, how coverage has spread over time, and how methods vary by place.

figs.title: Where the evidence is about
figs.caption: HFF studies naming each country, per 10 million people (log scale), shown on a diverging red–blue scale. North America, Western Europe, Australia and the Gulf are studied far more intensively per capita than South Asia or sub-Saharan Africa — 33.1 studies per 10M people is the median.

figs.title: Top 20 countries
figs.caption: Top 20 countries by study count — a multi-country study is counted once per country it names. United States of America leads with 9,415 study-country pairs, 3.4× China's 2,746.

figs.title: Study-country pairs by income group
figs.caption: Study-country pairs by income group. High income accounts for 19,792 study-country pairs, ahead of Upper middle income's 7,268.

figs.title: Geographic scope
figs.caption: Geographic scope of the analysis population. 81.3% of studies name a single country; the rest are multi-country or region/global in scope.

figs.title: Where the evidence is youngest
figs.caption: Share of a country's HFF studies published in 2018–2026, the later half of the window (global average 63%). Green = newer, faster-growing evidence base than average; brown = older. The evidence base is growing fastest in the Gulf and parts of Africa; several Latin American and Eastern European countries still carry a majority pre-2018 evidence base.

figs.title: When evidence reached each income group
figs.caption: Cumulative share of each World Bank income group's countries with ≥1 HFF study naming it, by year. Low income countries reached full coverage first, by 2016; every income group passed 95% coverage by 2021.

figs.title: Biggest producers vs. best-served
figs.caption: The 15 countries with the most HFF studies, ranked by total volume and again per 10 million people. A line falling to the right is a country whose standing rests on its size. India falls from rank 4 to 123 per capita; Australia climbs from 8 to 2.

figs.title: The dominant type of analysis
figs.caption: The most common type of analysis among each country's HFF studies (≥5 studies). Colour is the modal category. Quantitative is the modal type in 134 of 136 countries with enough studies to classify — Qualitative leads in only 2.

gallery.title: Geographic inequalities
gallery.blurb: Whether research is distributed in proportion to health needs: where evidence falls short of disease burden, how concentrated the L&MICs evidence base is, and where evidence deserts remain.

figs.title: Where high burden meets low evidence
figs.caption: Each country by its total disease burden (GBD 2023 DALYs) and its count of HFF studies naming it, in tertiles. Deep red = high burden, little research; blue = well-researched relative to burden; dark purple = high on both; cream = low on both. Angola, Chad, Iraq, Somalia, Algeria fall in the highest-burden, lowest-evidence cell — top third globally for disease burden, bottom third for HFF research volume.

figs.title: Research intensity against disease burden (map)
figs.caption: HFF studies naming each country, per 100,000 DALYs of disease burden. Blue: more research per unit of burden than the typical studied country; red: less. The median studied country has 0.97 studies per 100,000 DALYs — rich, small countries cluster far above that line, populous L&MICs far below it.

figs.title: Evidence deserts
figs.caption: Countries by number of HFF studies naming them, against the whole map of GBD 2023 burden. Red = a country that carries disease burden but has no HFF study at all. Equatorial Guinea, Djibouti have GBD burden data but zero HFF studies naming them.

figs.title: Research intensity vs. disease burden
figs.caption: Each point is a country: research intensity (studies per unit of disease burden) against total burden. The median high-income country has 12× more HFF studies per 100,000 DALYs than the median low-income country.

figs.title: Studies vs. a burden-proportional share
figs.caption: If research were proportional to disease burden, each country would hold a share of studies equal to its share of global DALYs. Bars right = below that expected count; left = above. India has about 4,446 fewer studies than a burden-proportional share; the largest surplus sits in United States of America (+7,959).

figs.title: Research relative to disease burden
figs.caption: Each point is a country. Values below zero indicate a smaller share of HFF studies than the country's share of global disease burden. 80 of 151 countries have a smaller research share than burden share; 60% of these are low- or lower-middle-income.

figs.title: L&MICs research share over time
figs.caption: Share of each year's single-country studies that are about low- and middle-income countries. It climbed from 26% in 2010 to 44% in 2025 — real progress, yet still far below the 83% of global disease burden L&MICs carry.

figs.title: Evidence concentration among L&MICs
figs.caption: Low- and middle-income countries ordered from least to most research per unit of disease burden. The five most-studied L&MICs hold 46% of the L&MICs evidence (Gini = 0.42).

figs.title: Adjusted odds ratios by income group
figs.caption: Adjusted odds ratios from two logistic models on single-country studies with a known income group. Reference group is high-income studies (OR=1). Adjusted for era; observational, so associations not causes. Low income studies have 0.28× the odds of a high-income study of using a quantitative analysis, and 0.08× the odds of Low income studies having a local author.

figs.title: Funding priority scorecard
figs.caption: Country research share divided by disease-burden share. Zero on the log2 scale means proportional coverage; negative values indicate less research relative to burden. Angola has the largest finite relative gap: its research share is 69x smaller than its burden share. No identified studies: Equatorial Guinea, Djibouti.

gallery.title: Research ownership & collaboration
gallery.blurb: Who produces research about different settings: local versus foreign authorship, collaboration across income groups, and where local research capacity could be strengthened.

figs.title: Who studies whom
figs.caption: Share of a country's single-country HFF studies that have at least one author based there. Blue = mostly domestic; red = mostly produced from outside. Madagascar has the lowest local-authorship share (36%) among countries with ≥5 studies with a known affiliation.

figs.title: Who leads research about each setting
figs.caption: Author-affiliation pattern of single-country studies, by the income group studied. Only 21% of Low income studies have a local-only author team, and 29% have no local author at all.

figs.title: Local authorship, by financing function
figs.caption: Share of single-country studies with a local author, by financing function tag. Only 89% of Capital investment: infrastructure studies have a local author, vs. 95% for Purchasing.

figs.title: Local authorship, by outcome domain
figs.caption: Authorship pattern of single-country studies reporting each outcome domain (row shares). Only 52% of Transparency and accountability studies have a local-only author team, the lowest share of any outcome domain.

figs.title: Cross-income co-authorship
figs.caption: Cross-income co-authorship of 25,175 studies with a known author-affiliation country. Ribbons: studies co-authored across two income groups (within-group studies excluded from the ribbons). Most evidence isn't cross-income at all: 15,226 studies are wholly high-income-authored; just 205 wholly low-income.

figs.title: Where to build local research capacity
figs.caption: Each country by disease burden and the share of its studies with a local author. Niger: high burden, only 40% local authorship.

gallery.title: Funders, fragility & outcomes
gallery.blurb: Who funds health financing research and what they prioritise, how research covers fragile and conflict-affected (FCAS) settings, and which outcomes studies measure. FCAS figures use the v5 fields added by the World Bank lookups (income group, region, FCAS) and the non-LLM themes for 'Other' outcomes.

figs.title: National governments fund most studies; industry funds few
figs.caption: Share of studies naming each type of funder, among studies that report any funder. National governments fund 52% of funded studies; pharmaceutical companies 5.8% and other private companies 1.4%.

figs.title: The top research funders
figs.caption: The most-named research funders across studies that report one, after merging name variants into a single entry. National Natural Science Foundation of China is named by 403 studies, more than any other funder.

figs.title: What each top funder pays for
figs.caption: Each top funder's financing-function tag mix (share of that funder's tag mentions; a study can carry more than one tag). 54% of Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality's financing-function tags are Purchasing, its most concentrated pairing among the top 12 funders.

figs.title: What each top funder's research finds
figs.caption: Outcome-domain mix of each top funder's studies (row shares; a study can carry more than one tag, so rows needn't sum to 100%). 78% of Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality-funded studies report Other, its most common outcome.

figs.title: Financing-function mix by top funder
figs.caption: Each top funder's financing-function tag mix (share of that funder's tag mentions; a study can carry more than one tag). 37% of Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality's financing-function tags are Purchasing, its most concentrated pairing among the top 8 funders.

figs.title: Which funders are gaining ground
figs.caption: Each top funder's share of that year's studies with a known funder, 2013–2025. National Natural Science Foundation of China's share rose +3.6pp from 2013–16 to 2022–25; Bill and Melinda Gates Foundation's fell -0.8pp.

figs.title: Funder to financing function to authorship
figs.caption: Each ribbon is a group of single-funder, single-country studies flowing from research funder, through primary financing function, to authorship pattern. National Natural Science Foundation of China funds the most studies in this flow (133), and 20 of all 412 studies shown (5%) have no local author at all.

figs.title: FCAS studies look more like low-income than high-income evidence
figs.caption: Share of studies in each setting that investigate each health-system goal. Versus high-income settings, FCAS studies focus more on financial protection (22% vs 8%) and less on efficiency in resource use (10% vs 16%).

figs.title: Nigeria and Ethiopia carry the FCAS evidence base
figs.caption: Studies about each fragile or conflict-affected country, top 20. 1,179 studies (3.2% of all) cover an FCAS country; Nigeria (297) and Ethiopia (184) appear in 41% of them.

figs.title: FCAS research is growing, but list changes exaggerate the jump
figs.caption: Studies on fragile or conflict-affected countries per year (top) and as a share of country-level studies (bottom). By each year's list the share tripled, 1.8% (2010-14) to 5.4% (2021-25); on a fixed set of countries it rose only from 5.5% to 7.2%.

figs.title: Most studies measure outcomes outside the named health-system goals
figs.caption: Share of studies investigating each outcome domain (a study can have several). 'Other' tags 57% of studies; among named goals, efficiency in resource use (14%) and financial protection (14%) lead.

figs.title: 'Other' outcomes are led by access and spending
figs.caption: Themes within the studies whose outcome domain is tagged 'Other'. Service use, access and coverage (22%) and levels, trends and drivers of spending, prices or funding (19%) are the largest themes.

figs.title: Health outcomes and financial protection gain ground
figs.caption: Share of each year's studies investigating each named health-system goal, 2010-2025. Improved level/distribution of health rose from 6% to 11% and financial protection from 10% to 14%; the rest barely moved.

gallery.title: Global financing context
gallery.blurb: Compare the research landscape with global health financing trends, including development assistance, national health spending and differences between countries.

figs.title: Development assistance for health, 1990–2030
figs.caption: Development assistance for health (DAH), 1990–2030 — solid is historical/preliminary, dashed is forecast. DAH fell 51% from its 2021 peak ($80bn) to $39bn in 2025, and is forecast to stay flat through 2030.

figs.title: The 2025 aid cuts, by source
figs.caption: Change in development assistance for health by source, 2024 → 2025. The US cut $9.5bn (-66%) — alone larger than the $11.0bn net drop across all sources combined.

figs.title: Health spending per person, by income group
figs.caption: Total health spending per person by World Bank income group, 2000–2030 (log scale; dashed = forecast). By 2025, the average person in a high-income country has $7,006 spent on their health — 174× the $40 in a low-income country, where per-person spending has fallen since 2020 ($52).

figs.title: Revenue-Raising research vs. real-world aid
figs.caption: Studies tagged Revenue Raising per year (this dataset) vs. global DAH (IHME), 2010–2025. Revenue-Raising research volume tracks the real DAH trend (correlation r=0.60) — both rose through the 2010s and have pulled back since the DAH peak.

figs.title: Every financing function vs. real-world aid
figs.caption: Growth index (2010–2011=100) for the 6 largest financing functions' study counts, vs. global DAH, 2010–2025. Pooling correlates with the DAH trend at r=0.61, the closest match among the 6 largest financing functions.

figs.title: Aid vs. evidence, by region
figs.caption: Share of global DAH (2022–24 average) vs. share of this dataset's study-country pairs, by region (income-first approximation of GBD super-regions). Sub-Saharan Africa receives 53% of DAH but only 12% of study-country pairs — the largest aid-to-evidence gap of any region.

figs.title: Research intensity vs. health spending, by country
figs.caption: Studies per million people vs. health spending per person (2025), by country. Log-log correlation r=0.61 across 149 matched countries — richer-spending countries are studied far more intensively per capita.

figs.title: Funding priority scorecard: health expenditure edition
figs.caption: Where research is most sparse relative to health spending (left, shaded), and the 15 countries with the largest absolute shortfall (right). United States of America alone is 5,474 studies short of a spending-proportional share — the largest gap of any country.

figs.title: Funding priority scorecard: burden, spending and research together
figs.caption: Disease burden vs. total health expenditure (left, shaded below the burden-proportional spending line); bubble size is each country's number of HFF studies, so a small bubble below the line is both underfunded and understudied. The 15 countries with the largest shortfall once burden AND spending capacity are both counted (right). Eritrea alone is 3,724 studies short of a share proportional to its burden-to-spending need — the largest gap of any country.

figs.title: Each function's research share vs. health spending
figs.caption: Each function's share of a country's classified research vs. health spending per person (log x-axis), one panel per function, with a linear trend line. Benefits decisions's share rises most with spending (r=0.45); Pooling's share falls most (r=-0.41).

figs.title: Ranked: function share vs. health spending
figs.caption: Correlation between each function's share of a country's research and log(health spending per person), across countries. Benefits decisions correlates at r=0.45; Pooling correlates at r=-0.41, the only clearly negative relationship.

figs.title: Ranked: function share vs. health spending (excluding USA)
figs.caption: Correlation between each function's share of a country's research and log(health spending per person), across countries. Studies mapped to the United States of America are excluded before country shares are recalculated. Benefits decisions correlates at r=0.47; Pooling correlates at r=-0.41, the only clearly negative relationship.

figs.title: Paired lollipop: all studies vs excluding USA
figs.caption: Paired lollipops compare each financing function's correlation between country-level research share and log(health spending per person): all studies versus the no-USA sensitivity analysis. The largest shift is for Purchasing (0.18 to 0.16).

figs.title: Correlation sensitivity: all studies vs excluding USA
figs.caption: Each point compares the correlation between a financing function's country-level research share and log(health spending per person) before and after removing all studies mapped to the United States of America. The largest shift is for Purchasing (0.18 to 0.16).

figs.title: Global financing-function mix: all studies vs excluding USA
figs.caption: Each point compares a financing function's share of all classified function tags in the full dataset versus after removing every study mapped to the United States of America. The largest shift is for Purchasing (-3.3 percentage points).

figs.title: Change in financing-function mix after excluding USA
figs.caption: Percentage-point change in each function's share of all classified function tags after removing every study mapped to the United States of America. Purchasing changes the most (-3.3 percentage points), showing how small the overall composition shift is.

figs.title: Financing-function mix by spending quartile
figs.caption: Financing-function mix (% of classified research) by health-spending quartile. Benefits decisions's share rises +12.9pp from the lowest- to highest-spending quartile, while Revenue Raising's share falls -9.0pp.

figs.title: Outcome-domain mix by spending quartile
figs.caption: Outcome-domain mix (% of classified research) by health-spending quartile. Other's share rises +8.8pp from the lowest- to highest-spending quartile, while Financial protection's share falls -8.4pp.

figs.title: Financing-function ranks, aid boom vs. bust
figs.caption: Rank of each function's average annual study count, DAH boom era (2015–2019) vs. bust era (2022–2025). No function changed rank between the two eras; Benefits decisions stayed first.

gallery.title: Open access & author countries
gallery.blurb: How much of the evidence is free to read, and where the authors behind it are based. Open-access status comes from OpenAlex via each study's DOI, so it covers the 29,793 studies (82%) that have one; author countries are the affiliation countries OpenAlex records.

figs.title: Where open-access research comes from
figs.caption: Open-access share of studies with at least one author based in each country. Blue = more open access than the average study; red = less. 79 of 98 author countries beat the average study (68%), which the large US output (63% open) pulls down. Among countries with ≥200 studies, Uganda is highest (91%) and Taiwan lowest (60%).

figs.title: Open access has become the norm
figs.caption: Share of each year's studies (with a DOI) that are open access. It rose from 42% in 2010 to 76% in 2025, passing half in 2012.

figs.title: Research with lower-income authors is more often open access
figs.caption: Open-access share by where a study's authors are based (dashed line: all studies). 73% of L&MICs-only author teams publish open access and 77% of mixed teams, vs 63% of teams based only in high-income countries.

figs.title: Authors in lower-income countries publish open access more often
figs.caption: Open-access share of studies with at least one author based in each country, the 25 most active author countries. Kenya tops the list (86%) and Taiwan is lowest (60%); the average is 77% across middle/low-income author countries vs 72% across high-income ones.
